Each style in the [Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.qmd) imitates a real band. This page says which
one: where the style came from, what the band's bass, comping and drums are copying (and what they leave
out), and the recordings to hear it played properly.

## Jazz

### Swing {#swing}

*Walking bass, the ride cymbal and syncopated comping*

[Open the Swing style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=swing){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The rhythm section of small-group jazz from the late 1930s onward: a bass that plays a note on
every beat, a drummer whose main voice is the ride cymbal (*ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a*) with the hi-hat
closing on 2 and 4, and a piano or guitar that "comps" (accompanies, complements): short chords placed
off the beat, answering the soloist instead of marking time.

#### A little history

In the 1920s the bass part of a jazz band was usually a tuba or a slapped string bass playing on beats 1
and 3 (the *two-beat* feel; see [Jazz ballad](#ballad)). In the Count Basie band of the mid-1930s,
bassist Walter Page walked four even beats a bar, guitarist Freddie Green strummed a quiet chord on every
beat, and drummer Jo Jones moved the time-keeping from the bass drum to the hi-hat. Basie himself played
sparse fills instead of a full stride left hand. That "All-American Rhythm Section" is where the modern
swing feel comes from.

In the 1940s bebop drummers (Kenny Clarke, then Max Roach) moved the pulse to the ride cymbal and used the
snare and bass drum for accents ("dropping bombs"). Pianists such as Bud Powell stopped playing on every
beat and comped in short syncopated stabs. By the late 1950s, rootless left-hand voicings (Bill Evans,
Wynton Kelly, Red Garland) became the standard piano sound: the bassist has the root, so the pianist plays
the 3rd, 7th and colour tones. That is the sound the band's piano uses here.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Walking*: root on beat 1, chord tones and scale steps, an approach note on beat 4.
- **Comping:** syncopated rhythms chosen from a set of figures (the Charleston, anticipations, and so on).
- **Drums:** ride-cymbal pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4, light comping on the snare.
- **Voicings:** rootless piano voicings, shell voicings on guitar. Players add unmarked 9ths and 13ths.

Real walking lines move far more freely than any rule set; the band's bassist is a beginner's model.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Count Basie Orchestra, *One O'Clock Jump* | 1937 | Walter Page's four-to-the-bar bass, Freddie Green's guitar, Jo Jones on hi-hat. |
| Count Basie, *Lester Leaps In* (Kansas City Seven) | 1939 | The same rhythm section in a small group behind Lester Young. |
| Miles Davis Quintet, *Oleo* (*Relaxin'*) | 1956 | Paul Chambers walking, Philly Joe Jones on the ride, Red Garland's comping. |
| Miles Davis, *Freddie Freeloader* (*Kind of Blue*) | 1959 | A jazz blues; Wynton Kelly's comping behind the horns. |
| Oscar Peterson Trio, *C Jam Blues* (*Night Train*) | 1962 | Ray Brown's walking bass at its most driving. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Tony Bennett & Lady Gaga, *Anything Goes* (*Cheek to Cheek*) | 2014 | A small group walking and swinging behind two singers. |
| Jon Batiste, *I Need You* (*We Are*) | 2021 | Swing-era rhythm in a Grammy-winning pop record. |

#### Sources

- Gunther Schuller, *The Swing Era* (Oxford, 1989), on the Basie rhythm section.
- Paul Berliner, *Thinking in Jazz* (Chicago, 1994), chapters on the rhythm section and comping.
- Mark Levine, *The Jazz Piano Book* (Sher, 1989), on rootless voicings.

### Jazz ballad {#ballad}

*Bass in two, long chords, quiet time*

[Open the Jazz ballad style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=ballad){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

A slow standard played by a jazz rhythm section: the bass on beats 1 and 3 (a *two-feel*), held chords on
the piano, and brushes stirring the snare or a soft ride. The band leaves room for the melody.

#### A little history

The two-feel is older than walking bass. New Orleans and 1920s dance bands put the tuba or string bass on
1 and 3, and when the bass began walking in the 1930s (see [Swing](#swing)), the two-feel stayed on as the
lighter gear: bands play the head of a tune in two and start walking for the solos. On ballads it never
has to leave. Brushes, used on drums since the 1920s, became the ballad sound through drummers such as Jo
Jones and later Philly Joe Jones and Ed Thigpen. Pianists filled the long chords with the rich voicings
that came from Ellington, Billy Strayhorn and later Bill Evans.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Two-feel*: root on 1, fifth on 3, now and then a pickup into the next bar.
- **Comping:** long held chords (*pad*).
- **Drums:** quiet time. **Voicings:** rootless, with unmarked extensions.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Coleman Hawkins, *Body and Soul* | 1939 | The tenor ballad everyone learned; the band barely there. |
| Miles Davis, *'Round Midnight* (*'Round About Midnight*) | 1956 | Harmon mute over Paul Chambers in two. |
| Bill Evans Trio, *My Foolish Heart* (*Waltz for Debby*) | 1961 | Paul Motian's brushes; Scott LaFaro's bass. |
| John Coltrane, *Ballads* | 1962 | A whole album of the form; McCoy Tyner's voicings. |
| John Coltrane & Johnny Hartman, *My One and Only Love* | 1963 | Ballad accompaniment behind a singer. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Tony Bennett & Amy Winehouse, *Body and Soul* | 2011 | The same tune as Hawkins, with a quiet trio under the voices. |
| Laufey, *Valentine* (*Everything I Know About Love*) | 2022 | A jazz-ballad band under a young pop singer. |

#### Sources

- Paul Berliner, *Thinking in Jazz* (Chicago, 1994), on the two-feel and on brushes.
- Ted Gioia, *The Jazz Standards* (Oxford, 2012), entries for the tunes above.

### Boogaloo {#boogaloo}

*Straight eighths, a bass riff and chord stabs, from soul jazz*

[Open the Boogaloo style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=boogaloo){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

A jazz band playing straight (not swung) eighth notes over a repeated bass figure, with piano or organ
chords locked to the riff and a backbeat on the drums. It sits between hard bop, R&B and Latin music.

#### A little history

The word covers two related things from the mid-1960s. **Latin boogaloo** was a New York dance music that
mixed Cuban son and mambo with R&B; Joe Cuba's *Bang! Bang!* (1966) and Pete Rodríguez's *I Like It Like
That* (1967) were hits. In jazz, **soul jazz** players on labels like Blue Note took up the same straight
eighths. Herbie Hancock's *Watermelon Man* (1962) and Lee Morgan's *The Sidewinder* (recorded 1963) came first,
and Lou Donaldson's *Alligator Bogaloo* (1967) put the name on the jazz version. Drummers such as Idris
Muhammad and Bernard Purdie played a backbeat with busy sixteenth-note hi-hats; the tunes were often blues
forms over one riff. Mongo Santamaría's cover of *Watermelon Man* (1963) carried the Latin side, with
congas, back into the charts, which is why the band adds a conga tumbao.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Boogaloo riff*: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, fifth and flat seventh on 4.
- **Comping:** stabs on the same rhythm as the riff.
- **Drums:** straight-eighth backbeat. **Congas:** a tumbao.
- **Voicings:** rootless jazz voicings.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Herbie Hancock, *Watermelon Man* (*Takin' Off*) | 1962 | The riff in the bass and piano left hand; Billy Higgins' even eighths. |
| Mongo Santamaría, *Watermelon Man* | 1963 | The same tune with congas and a Latin band. |
| Lee Morgan, *The Sidewinder* | 1963 rec., 1964 | A 24-bar blues on a boogaloo groove; the record that sold Blue Note on the feel. |
| Joe Cuba Sextet, *Bang! Bang!* | 1966 | Latin boogaloo: party noise over a piano montuno. |
| Lou Donaldson, *Alligator Bogaloo* | 1967 | Improvised as filler in the studio; Lonnie Smith's organ, George Benson's guitar, Idris Muhammad (then Leo Morris) on drums. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Us3, *Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia)* | 1993 | Built on Herbie Hancock's *Cantaloupe Island* (1964): the soul-jazz riff under hip-hop drums. |
| Herbie Hancock, *Watermelon Man* (*Head Hunters*) | 1973 | The same tune redone as funk, for comparison. |

#### Sources

- [Blue Note, "Lou Donaldson: the fortuitously funky Alligator Bogaloo"](https://www.bluenote.com/spotlight/lou-donaldson-the-fortuitous-funk-of-alligato/)
- [Wikipedia, *Alligator Bogaloo*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator_Bogaloo): recorded 7 April 1967, Van Gelder Studio.
- Juan Flores, *From Bomba to Hip-Hop* (Columbia, 2000), chapter on Latin boogaloo.

### Ragtime {#ragtime}

*A march for the piano, with the melody ragged against it*

[Open the Ragtime style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=ragtime){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Composed piano music from about 1895 to 1920, built like a march: several 16-bar strains, a left hand
that plays a bass note on the beat and a chord off it, and a right hand whose melody is syncopated
("ragged") against that steady left hand. Its eighth notes are straight, not swung.

Ragtime is where [stride](#stride) came from: the stride left hand is the ragtime left hand, played
faster and swung, with songs and the blues in place of written rags. The lesson
[Two Left Hands](../lessons/stride-boogie.qmd) plays the two one after the other.

#### A little history

Ragtime grew among Black pianists in the saloons and dance halls of the Mississippi valley in the
1890s, and became the first African American music to sell across the country, mostly as sheet music
for parlour pianos. Scott Joplin's *Maple Leaf Rag* (1899), published in Sedalia, Missouri, sold
hundreds of thousands of copies. Joplin, James Scott and Joseph Lamb wrote the "classic rags"; Tin Pan
Alley turned out ragtime songs by the thousand. Bands played rags too, and ragtime fed straight into
early jazz in New Orleans and into Harlem stride.

It was largely forgotten until the 1970s, when Joshua Rifkin's recordings of Joplin and the film *The
Sting* (1973), with Marvin Hamlisch's arrangement of *The Entertainer*, brought it back.

#### The band's version

- **Comping:** *Stride*: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 and the chord on 2 and 4, in straight
  time.
- **Bass:** *Root and fifth* on 1 and 3, like the tuba in a march band.
- **Drums:** *Boom-chick*: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
- **Voicings:** plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

A rag is written down, and its right-hand melody is the point. The band plays only the left hand's
pattern; the ragged melody is yours.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Scott Joplin, *Maple Leaf Rag* (piano roll) | 1916 | Joplin's own playing, as near as a roll allows. |
| Jelly Roll Morton, *Maple Leaf Rag* (Library of Congress) | 1938 | Morton showing how New Orleans turned the rag into jazz. |
| Joshua Rifkin, *Piano Rags by Scott Joplin* | 1970 | Rags played as written, slowly, as Joplin asked. |
| Marvin Hamlisch, *The Entertainer* (*The Sting*) | 1973 | The record that brought ragtime back. |

#### Sources

- Edward A. Berlin, *Ragtime: A Musical and Cultural History* (California, 1980).
- Rudi Blesh and Harriet Janis, *They All Played Ragtime* (Knopf, 1950).
- Gunther Schuller, *Early Jazz* (Oxford, 1968).

### Stride Piano {#stride}

*A left hand that leaps: bass note, chord, bass note, chord*

[Open the Stride piano style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=stride){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Solo piano music from Harlem in the late 1910s to the 1930s. The left hand does the work of a whole rhythm
section: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4, the hand
leaping ("striding") between them on every beat. The right hand plays the melody, decorated, over it.

Stride and [boogie-woogie](#boogie) grew up side by side: both are piano music for dancing at parties,
both put a whole band into the left hand, and both feed into swing. They differ in what the left hand
does. The lesson [Two Left Hands](../lessons/stride-boogie.qmd) plays them side by side.

#### A little history

Stride comes out of [ragtime](#ragtime). A Scott Joplin rag already has the oom-pah left hand, written as a march.
In New York around the First World War, pianists such as James P. Johnson, Luckey Roberts and Willie
"The Lion" Smith played it faster and swung it, took it from rags to popular songs and the blues, and
added runs, tenths and cross-rhythms. They played at *rent parties*, where tenants paid the rent by
charging for food, drink and music, and in *cutting contests* against each other. Johnson's *Carolina
Shout* was the test piece: Duke Ellington learned it from a piano roll, slowed down.

Johnson's pupil Fats Waller made stride popular on records and radio, from 1934 with a small band,
*Fats Waller and His Rhythm*: bass, drums and guitar playing in two under the piano's left hand. That
is the sound this style copies. Art Tatum took stride to its technical limit; Count Basie began as a
stride pianist and pared it down to almost nothing; Thelonious Monk kept stride passages in his playing
all his life.

Johnson also wrote *Charleston* (1923). Its rhythm, a long note on 1 and a short one on the and of 2, is
the [Charleston comping figure](../lessons/patterns/chords.qmd#chords-charleston) jazz pianists still use.

#### The band's version

- **Comping:** *Stride*: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 (the root as an octave where a chord
  starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. On the guitar it
  is plain boom-chick.
- **Bass:** *Two-feel*: half notes on 1 and 3, with the piano's left hand.
- **Drums:** *Jazz time*, lightly.
- **Voicings:** plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Real stride left hands reach for tenths, walk them up and down between chords, and break the pattern for
a run; the right hand carries the tune. The band's pianist keeps the pattern and plays no melody. That is
your part.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| James P. Johnson, *Carolina Shout* | 1921 | The test piece of the Harlem pianists. |
| Fats Waller, *Handful of Keys* | 1929 | Stride at speed, solo. |
| Fats Waller, *Ain't Misbehavin'* (solo piano) | 1929 | The same left hand under a song. |
| Fats Waller and His Rhythm, *I'm Gonna Sit Right Down and Write Myself a Letter* | 1935 | Stride piano with bass and drums: this style. |
| Art Tatum, *Tiger Rag* | 1933 | Stride as virtuoso display. |
| Willie "The Lion" Smith, *Echoes of Spring* | 1939 | A gentler, more harmonic stride. |

#### Sources

- Gunther Schuller, *Early Jazz* (Oxford, 1968), on James P. Johnson and the Harlem pianists.
- Willie "The Lion" Smith with George Hoefer, *Music on My Mind* (Doubleday, 1964), on rent parties and cutting contests.
- Scott E. Brown, *James P. Johnson: A Case of Mistaken Identity* (Scarecrow, 1986).
- Riccardo Scivales, *Jazz Piano: The Left Hand* (Ekay, 1990), on stride and boogie-woogie left hands.

### Boogie-Woogie {#boogie}

*A left hand that walks: eight to the bar on the blues*

[Open the Boogie-woogie style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=boogie){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Blues piano with a left hand that never stops: eight notes to the bar, swung, repeating one figure up
and down the chord while the right hand plays riffs, tremolos and blue notes against it. It is almost
always a 12-bar blues.

Boogie-woogie and [stride](#stride) are close relations: both are piano music for dancing at
parties, both put a band into the left hand, and the same pianists often played both. Stride's left
hand leaps between bass and chord on the beats; boogie-woogie's walks along the bass in eighth notes.
The lesson [Two Left Hands](../lessons/stride-boogie.qmd) plays them side by side.

#### A little history

The style began in the lumber, turpentine and railroad camps of Texas and Louisiana in the first years
of the 1900s, played on "barrelhouse" pianos in the camps' bars, and travelled north with the
migration. In Chicago in the 1920s it was the music of rent parties, as stride was in Harlem. Pinetop
Smith's *Pine Top's Boogie Woogie* (1928) gave the style its name; Jimmy Yancey, Meade Lux Lewis and
Albert Ammons played it in Chicago.

In December 1938 the producer John Hammond put Ammons, Lewis and Pete Johnson on stage at Carnegie Hall
in the *From Spirituals to Swing* concert, and boogie-woogie became a national craze. Big bands
arranged it (Count Basie's *Boogie Woogie*, Tommy Dorsey's version of Pinetop's piece), and the
Andrews Sisters sang it. Its eight-to-the-bar bass went into [jump blues](#jump), rhythm and blues and early
rock and roll: Chuck Berry's guitar plays a boogie left hand.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Boogie-woogie*: swung eighths walking up the chord and back down, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th
  6th 5th 3rd, every bar. The pianist's left hand, on the bass.
- **Comping:** *Boogie-woogie right hand*: a two-bar riff of short swung chords against the bass.
- **Drums:** *Blues shuffle*: swung eighths on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
- **Voicings:** plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Boogie-woogie pianists have dozens of left-hand patterns (rolling octaves, the Yancey bass, broken
sixths) and their right hands play the lead. The band's bassist has one pattern and its pianist one
riff, so a melody or a solo on top is your part.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Meade Lux Lewis, *Honky Tonk Train Blues* | 1927 | A train in the left hand, cross-rhythms in the right. |
| Pinetop Smith, *Pine Top's Boogie Woogie* | 1928 | The record that named the style; Smith calls out to the dancers. |
| Albert Ammons, *Boogie Woogie Stomp* | 1936 | The walking left hand at full power. |
| Count Basie, *Boogie Woogie* (with Jimmy Rushing) | 1936 | Boogie-woogie from a small swing band. |
| Big Joe Turner and Pete Johnson, *Roll 'Em Pete* | 1938 | Boogie-woogie under a blues shouter: a short step to rock and roll. |
| Jimmy Yancey, *Yancey Stomp* | 1939 | A lighter, older Chicago style. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Jerry Lee Lewis, *Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On* | 1957 | The boogie left hand in rock and roll. |

#### Sources

- Peter J. Silvester, *A Left Hand Like God: A History of Boogie-Woogie Piano* (Quartet, 1988).
- Ted Gioia, *The History of Jazz* (Oxford, 1997), on Chicago and the 1938 Carnegie Hall concert.
- Riccardo Scivales, *Jazz Piano: The Left Hand* (Ekay, 1990), on stride and boogie-woogie left hands.

### Jump Blues {#jump}

*Boogie-woogie for a small band, loud, on the backbeat*

[Open the Jump blues style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=jump){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Up-tempo blues for dancing, played by small bands of the 1940s: a rhythm section, two or three horns
riffing together, and a singer. The bass plays the [boogie-woogie](#boogie) left hand, the drums play
a shuffle with a hard backbeat on 2 and 4, and the horns and piano play short riffs. It is the bridge
from swing and boogie-woogie to rhythm and blues and rock and roll.

#### A little history

When the big bands became too costly during the Second World War, many of their players formed small
groups that kept the swing bands' riffs and the boogie-woogie bass but played them louder, on the
backbeat, for dancers and jukeboxes. Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five were the most popular: *Caldonia*
(1945) and *Choo Choo Ch'Boogie* (1946) topped the race-record charts, which *Billboard* renamed
*rhythm and blues* in 1949. Big Joe Turner, Wynonie Harris, Roy Brown and Amos Milburn sang it; Lionel
Hampton's *Flying Home* gave it a honking tenor sax. By the early 1950s the same music, with an electric
guitar in front, was being called rock and roll.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Boogie-woogie*: swung eighths, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th 6th 5th 3rd.
- **Comping:** *Boogie-woogie right hand*: a two-bar riff of short swung chords.
- **Drums:** *Jump blues*: the shuffle on the cymbal, the kick feathered on every beat, a loud snare on
  2 and 4.
- **Voicings:** plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

The horns are what most people remember of a jump band, and the band has none. Play the riffs yourself,
or sing.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Lionel Hampton, *Flying Home* | 1942 | Illinois Jacquet's tenor solo, the model for every honking sax after it. |
| Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five, *Caldonia* | 1945 | Riffing horns over a shuffle; the singer as entertainer. |
| Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five, *Choo Choo Ch'Boogie* | 1946 | A boogie bass under a country-flavoured song. |
| Roy Brown, *Good Rockin' Tonight* | 1947 | The backbeat that rock and roll took. |
| Big Joe Turner, *Shake, Rattle and Roll* | 1954 | Jump blues on the edge of rock and roll. |

#### Sources

- Arnold Shaw, *Honkers and Shouters: The Golden Years of Rhythm and Blues* (Collier, 1978).
- John Chilton, *Let the Good Times Roll: The Story of Louis Jordan and His Music* (Michigan, 1994).

## Latin

### Bossa nova {#bossa}

*Root-and-fifth bass, a two-bar comping pattern and the bossa clave*

[Open the Bossa nova style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=bossa){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Brazilian song style from Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s: samba slowed and quietened for a voice and a
nylon-string guitar. The guitarist's thumb plays the bass on beats 1 and 3 (in 2/4 counting, the two
beats of the bar) while the fingers play syncopated chords that repeat over two bars.

#### A little history

Samba's percussion section (the surdo bass drum, tamborim, agogô) was too loud for the small apartments and
clubs of Copacabana. João Gilberto moved the parts onto the guitar: the thumb took the surdo, the fingers
took the tamborim's syncopations. His single *Chega de Saudade* (1958, song by Antônio Carlos Jobim and
Vinícius de Moraes) is usually called the first bossa nova record. Jobim's harmony (major sevenths, ninths,
chromatic inner lines) came from jazz and from Debussy and Ravel.

American jazz musicians took it up after Charlie Byrd and Stan Getz's *Jazz Samba* (1962). *Getz/Gilberto*
(recorded 1963, released 1964), with Astrud Gilberto singing *The Girl from Ipanema*, made it a world
style. Jazz drummers turned the guitar's rhythm into the brush or cross-stick pattern the band plays: a
two-bar figure close to the son clave, over a steady bass drum on 1 and 3.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** root and fifth with pickups. **Comping:** the two-bar pattern.
- **Drums:** bossa clave on the cross-stick. **Voicings:** jazz voicings with added 9ths.
- **Feel:** straight eighths. Bossa never swings.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| João Gilberto, *Chega de Saudade* | 1958 | The guitar rhythm that started it. |
| Stan Getz & Charlie Byrd, *Desafinado* (*Jazz Samba*) | 1962 | The first American hit version. |
| Stan Getz & João Gilberto, *The Girl from Ipanema* | 1964 | Milton Banana's drums; Jobim on piano. |
| Antônio Carlos Jobim, *Wave* | 1967 | Jobim's own arrangement, Ron Carter on bass. |
| Elis Regina & Tom Jobim, *Águas de Março* | 1974 | A later, freer bossa groove. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Bebel Gilberto, *Samba da Bênção* (*Tanto Tempo*) | 2000 | João Gilberto's daughter: bossa with electronic beats. |
| Laufey, *From the Start* | 2023 | A bossa groove that went viral: guitar rhythm, cross-stick, root-and-fifth bass. |

#### Sources

- Ruy Castro, *Bossa Nova: The Story of the Brazilian Music That Seduced the World* (A Cappella, 2000).
- Chris McGowan and Ricardo Pessanha, *The Brazilian Sound* (Temple, 2009 ed.).

### Son montuno {#montuno}

*Tumbao bass, the montuno, son clave and congas*

[Open the Son montuno style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=montuno){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The groove of Cuban son and of salsa: a two-bar repeating piano figure (the *montuno* or *guajeo*), a
bass that plays ahead of the beat (the *tumbao*), and a clave pattern every part is fitted to.

#### A little history

**Son** grew up in eastern Cuba and reached Havana around 1910-20, played by small groups on tres (a guitar
with three doubled strings), guitar, bongó, maracas, claves and a *marímbula* or bass. The second half of
a son, the *montuno*, is a vamp where a lead singer improvises against a chorus. In the late 1930s and
1940s Arsenio Rodríguez enlarged the group into the *conjunto*: piano, trumpets, and a conga. He is credited
with the anticipated bass: the bass skips beat 1 and lands on the *and of 2* and on 4, so that each
chord is heard a little before the bar it belongs to. Mambo bands (Pérez Prado, Machito) and the New York
salsa of the 1960s and '70s (Eddie Palmieri, Fania Records) built on the same parts.

**Clave** is the two-bar rhythm (3-2: three hits then two; or 2-3) that the parts are written around. The
band plays 2-3.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** tumbao, anticipating each bar. **Comping:** the two-bar montuno.
- **Drums:** clave. **Congas:** a tumbao moving to the second drum every other bar.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Septeto Nacional (Ignacio Piñeiro), *Échale salsita* | 1930 | Early son with the old sextet line-up. |
| Arsenio Rodríguez y su Conjunto, *Dame un cachito pa' huelé* | 1946 | The conjunto sound and the anticipated bass. |
| Machito and his Afro-Cubans, *Tanga* | composed 1943, recorded later in the 1940s | Son and mambo meeting big-band jazz. |
| Eddie Palmieri, *Azúcar Pa' Ti* | 1965 | The piano montuno stretched out over a long vamp. |
| Buena Vista Social Club, *Chan Chan* | 1997 | Compay Segundo's son; easy to count the clave. |

### Cha-cha {#chacha}

*A steady bell and the cha-cha-chá on 3, the and of 3, and 4*

[Open the Cha-cha style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=chacha){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

A medium-tempo Cuban dance rhythm, steadier and simpler than mambo, with a cowbell on every beat and the
three quick steps (*cha-cha-chá*) on beat 3, the and of 3, and beat 4.

#### A little history

Violinist Enrique Jorrín, of the *charanga* orchestra Orquesta América, wrote *La engañadora* (1951, recorded
1953). The orchestra's dancers found its rhythm easier than the danzón-mambo, and the steps' scuffing sound
named the dance. Charangas played it on flute, violins, piano, bass, timbales, güiro and conga; Orquesta
Aragón made it famous across Latin America. By the late 1950s it was a ballroom dance in the US and Europe,
and American pop recorded "cha-cha" versions of everything.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** the cha-cha bass line. **Comping:** chords on the cha-cha figure.
- **Drums:** a bell on the beats. **Congas:** a tumbao. **Voicings:** plain triads and sevenths.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Orquesta América, *La engañadora* | 1953 | The first cha-cha-chá. |
| Orquesta Aragón, *El bodeguero* | mid-1950s (year not checked) | The charanga sound: flute, violins, güiro. |
| Tito Puente, *Oye Cómo Va* | 1963 | A cha-cha that Santana later made a rock hit (1970). |
| Cal Tjader, *Soul Sauce (Guachi Guaro)* | 1965 | Latin jazz on a cha-cha groove. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Santana, *Oye Como Va* | 1970 | Tito Puente's cha-cha as Latin rock. |
| Michael Bublé, *Sway* | 2003 | A 1950s mambo/cha-cha song in a pop big-band arrangement. |

#### Sources

- Ned Sublette, *Cuba and Its Music* (2004), on Jorrín and the charanga.
- Sue Steward, *¡Música!: Salsa, Rumba, Merengue and More* (Chronicle, 1999).

### Tango {#tango}

*The habanera rhythm in the bass and chords*

[Open the Tango style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=tango){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The dance music of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, in 2/4 or 4/4, played here on its oldest rhythm: the
*habanera* (dotted eighth, sixteenth, two eighths), which also underlies the 3+3+2 of a lot of later pop.

#### A little history

The **habanera** was a Cuban song and dance of the mid-1800s that spread through Spain, Mexico and the
Río de la Plata ports (Bizet borrowed one for *Carmen*, 1875). In the poor neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires
in the 1880s and '90s it mixed with the milonga, Spanish and Italian song, and African Argentine candombe
into the tango. Early groups were flute, violin and guitar; the bandoneón (a German button accordion)
arrived around 1900 and became the tango's voice. Carlos Gardel's *Mi noche triste* (1917) began the sung
tango. The 1940s *orquestas típicas* (Juan D'Arienzo, Aníbal Troilo, Osvaldo Pugliese) moved to a driving
*marcato* in four; from the 1950s Astor Piazzolla's *nuevo tango* added jazz and classical counterpoint.

The band plays the habanera rhythm, the older and more widely useful of tango's rhythms; the four-beat
*marcato* of the dance orchestras is not modelled.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Ángel Villoldo, *El Choclo* (many recordings) | 1903 | An early tango built on the habanera. |
| Carlos Gardel, *Mi noche triste* | 1917 | The first sung tango. |
| Juan D'Arienzo, *La cumparsita* | 1937 | The 1930s marcato for dancing. |
| Osvaldo Pugliese, *La yumba* | 1946 | The heavy *yumba* beat. |
| Astor Piazzolla, *Adiós Nonino* | 1959 | Nuevo tango. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Gotan Project, *Santa María (Del Buen Ayre)* | 2001 | Electronic tango: bandoneón over programmed beats. |
| *El Tango de Roxanne* (*Moulin Rouge!*) | 2001 | Tango in a film musical, habanera rhythm under a pop song. |

#### Sources

- Simon Collier et al., *¡Tango! The Dance, the Song, the Story* (Thames & Hudson, 1995).
- Robert Farris Thompson, *Tango: The Art History of Love* (Pantheon, 2005).

## Caribbean

### Calypso {#calypso}

*Root-and-fifth bass with chords on every off-beat*

[Open the Calypso style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=calypso){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The topical song of Trinidad: a singer (the *calypsonian*) with a witty, often political lyric over a
bouncing 2/4, with a strummed guitar or cuatro, a bass on root and fifth, and chords on the off-beats.

#### A little history

Calypso (earlier *kaiso*) grew out of the songs of Trinidad's Carnival in the 1800s: the *chantwell*
leading call-and-response songs in French Creole, stick-fighting songs, and the music of the Spanish
Venezuelan string bands. By the 1910s-20s it was sung in English and recorded in New York. Calypso tents
competed each Carnival season, and singers took grand names: Atilla the Hun, Roaring Lion, Lord Invader,
Lord Kitchener, the Mighty Sparrow. Lord Invader's *Rum and Coca-Cola* (sung at the 1943 Carnival) became an American hit for the
Andrews Sisters in 1945, and Invader later won a lawsuit over its royalties; and Harry Belafonte's album *Calypso* (1956) was the first LP to sell a million
copies. Jamaica's **mento** is a cousin, and in the 1970s Lord Shorty mixed calypso with Indian rhythms
into **soca**, now Carnival's main music.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Root and fifth*. **Comping:** chords on every off-beat. **Drums:** a calypso beat.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Lord Invader, *Rum and Coca-Cola* | 1946 (New York) | His own record of the 1943 Carnival song the Andrews Sisters covered. |
| Lord Kitchener, *London Is the Place for Me* | 1951 | Calypso of the Windrush generation in Britain. |
| Harry Belafonte, *Day-O (The Banana Boat Song)* | 1956 | Jamaican folk song, calypso arrangement. |
| The Mighty Sparrow, *Jean and Dinah* | 1956 | The Carnival Road March that made Sparrow's name. |
| Lord Shorty, *Endless Vibrations* | 1974 | Early soca. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Arrow, *Hot Hot Hot* | 1982 | Soca: the calypso off-beats sped up for a worldwide party hit. |
| Harry Belafonte, *Jump in the Line* (in *Beetlejuice*) | 1961, film 1988 | A calypso brought back to a new audience by a film. |

#### Sources

- Donald R. Hill, *Calypso Calaloo: Early Carnival Music in Trinidad* (Florida, 1993).
- [Wikipedia, *London Is the Place for Me*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Is_the_Place_for_Me): sung on arrival in 1948, recorded 1951.
- Gordon Rohlehr, *Calypso and Society in Pre-Independence Trinidad* (1990).

### Ska / reggae {#reggae}

*Off-beat chords over a one-drop*

[Open the Ska / reggae style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=reggae){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Jamaican popular music since about 1960: guitar and keyboard chords on the off-beats (the *skank*), a bass
that carries the melody of the groove, and, in reggae, a **one-drop** drum beat with nothing on beat 1 and
the kick and snare (or rim) together on beat 3.

#### A little history

**Ska** (c. 1960-66) came from Jamaican musicians playing American R&B for sound systems and stressing
the off-beat; studio bands such as the Skatalites played it fast with horns. Around 1966 the tempo slowed
into **rocksteady**, with the bass more prominent (Alton Ellis, the Paragons). By 1968 the beat had
changed again into **reggae**: Toots and the Maytals' *Do the Reggay* (1968) is one of the first records
to use the word. Drummer Carlton Barrett of Bob Marley's Wailers made the one-drop the standard reggae
beat, and Island Records' *Catch a Fire* (1973) took the Wailers worldwide. Later strands include dub,
roots, lovers rock, dancehall (see [Reggaeton](#reggaeton)) and Britain's 2 Tone ska revival (c. 1979).

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Roots on every beat*, plainer than a real reggae bass line, which moves and leaves gaps.
- **Comping:** off-beat chords. **Drums:** one-drop.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| The Skatalites, *Guns of Navarone* | 1965 | Ska: fast, horns, the off-beat guitar. |
| Alton Ellis, *Rock Steady* | 1967 | The slower rocksteady groove. |
| Desmond Dekker & the Aces, *Israelites* | 1968 | Early reggae; a UK number one in 1969. |
| Toots and the Maytals, *Do the Reggay* | 1968 | The name on a record. |
| Bob Marley & the Wailers, *Stir It Up* (*Catch a Fire*) | 1973 | Carlton Barrett's one-drop, Aston Barrett's bass. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Sublime, *Santeria* | 1996 | Off-beat guitar and a one-drop feel in American alt-rock. |
| No Doubt, *Underneath It All* | 2001 | Recorded in Jamaica with Sly & Robbie. |
| Damian Marley, *Welcome to Jamrock* | 2005 | Modern roots reggae. |
| Rihanna, *Man Down* | 2011 | A one-drop under a pop singer. |

#### Sources

- Lloyd Bradley, *Bass Culture: When Reggae Was King* (Penguin, 2000).
- David Katz, *Solid Foundation: An Oral History of Reggae* (Bloomsbury, 2003).

### Reggaeton {#reggaeton}

*The dembow drum pattern under long chords, the bass on a 3+3+2*

[Open the Reggaeton style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=reggaeton){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Spanish-language dance music from Puerto Rico and Panama, built on the **dembow**: the kick on every beat,
and the snare on the last sixteenth of beat 1 and the and of 2 (and again in beats 3 and 4), a 3+3+2 in
sixteenths over each half bar, under long synth chords and a rapped or sung vocal.

#### A little history

The rhythm is named after Shabba Ranks' Jamaican dancehall record *Dem Bow* (1990), whose riddim (the
backing track, by Steely & Clevie, built on their *Poco Man Jam*) was copied everywhere. In Panama,
artists such as El General sang Spanish lyrics over dancehall riddims (*reggae en español*). In Puerto Rico
in the 1990s DJ Playero and others made underground mixtapes on the same beats; the name *reggaeton* took
hold around the turn of the century. Daddy Yankee's *Gasolina* (2004) was the international breakthrough,
Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee's *Despacito* (2017) one of the most-streamed songs ever, and Bad Bunny the
genre's biggest star of the 2020s.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *3+3+2 (tresillo)*. **Comping:** long held chords. **Drums:** dembow.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Shabba Ranks, *Dem Bow* | 1990 | The record the rhythm is named after. |
| El General, *Te Ves Buena* | 1991 | Reggae en español from Panama. |
| Daddy Yankee, *Gasolina* | 2004 | The breakthrough. |
| Luis Fonsi ft. Daddy Yankee, *Despacito* | 2017 | Dembow under a pop song. |
| Bad Bunny, *Tití Me Preguntó* | 2022 | The current sound. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Karol G & Nicki Minaj, *Tusa* | 2019 | Dembow under a pop-ballad chord loop. |

#### Sources

- Raquel Z. Rivera, Wayne Marshall and Deborah Pacini Hernandez (eds.), *Reggaeton* (Duke, 2009).
- Petra R. Rivera-Rideau, *Remixing Reggaetón* (Duke, 2015).

## Folk, rock and pop

### Straight-eighth rock {#rock}

*Root eighths, down-up strumming and a backbeat*

[Open the Straight-eighth rock style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=rock){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The basic rock band: drums with a snare **backbeat** on 2 and 4 and even eighth notes on the hi-hat, an
electric bass on the root in eighths, and guitar strumming every eighth note.

#### A little history

Rhythm and blues of the late 1940s and early '50s was mostly shuffled (swung) eighths. Through the 1950s,
records by Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Ray Charles mixed straight eighths in, and by the early 1960s
even eighths were the norm in rock and soul; Alexander Stewart traces the shift through New Orleans
drummers such as Earl Palmer. The backbeat came from gospel handclaps and R&B. The British Invasion, then
punk's down-stroke eighths (the Ramones, 1976) and new wave, kept the plain driving eighths at the centre
of the style.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Root eighths*. **Comping:** down-up eighths on the guitar. **Drums:** a backbeat whose kick
  varies from bar to bar. Chords are **pushed** (they arrive an eighth early) the way rock bands do.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Little Richard, *Lucille* | 1957 | Often cited as an early straight-eighth rock and roll record. |
| Chuck Berry, *Johnny B. Goode* | 1958 | The guitar boogie that became rock rhythm guitar. |
| The Kinks, *You Really Got Me* | 1964 | Power chords and driving eighths. |
| Ramones, *Blitzkrieg Bop* | 1976 | Eighths on everything. |
| U2, *With or Without You* | 1987 | Adam Clayton's root eighths, the whole song. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| The Strokes, *Last Nite* | 2001 | Garage-rock eighths on guitar and bass. |
| The Killers, *Mr. Brightside* | 2003 | Driving eighths the whole song. |
| Arctic Monkeys, *I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor* | 2005 | Fast straight eighths and a backbeat. |

#### Sources

- Alexander Stewart, "'Funky Drummer': New Orleans, James Brown and the rhythmic transformation of American
  popular music", *Popular Music* 19/3 (2000).
- Robert Palmer, *Rock & Roll: An Unruly History* (Harmony, 1995).

### Emo / pop-punk {#emo}

*Palm-muted power chords that open up in the chorus*

[Open the Emo / pop-punk style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=emo){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Guitar-band rock at punk tempos with melodic, often confessional singing: a distorted guitar chugging
palm-muted power chords in the verse, ringing open in the chorus, over root eighths and a rock beat, with
half-time choruses and breakdowns.

#### A little history

**Emo** ("emotional hardcore") began in Washington, D.C., in 1985 with Rites of Spring and Embrace, who
took hardcore punk's speed into more personal songs. The 1990s brought a quieter, intricate "Midwest emo"
(Cap'n Jazz, American Football). **Pop-punk** runs from the Buzzcocks and the Ramones to Green Day's
*Dookie* (1994), which sold millions, then Blink-182. Around 2000-2007 the two merged into a mainstream
sound: Jimmy Eat World, My Chemical Romance, Fall Out Boy, Paramore. It came back in the 2020s, from
Olivia Rodrigo to a revival of the bands themselves.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Root eighths*. **Comping:** palm-muted chugging in verses, open strumming in Chorus bars.
- **Drums:** rock backbeat; mark bars Half-time for a half-time chorus or breakdown.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Green Day, *Basket Case* | 1994 | Pop-punk: muted verse, open chorus. |
| Blink-182, *All the Small Things* | 1999 | Root eighths and simple power chords. |
| Jimmy Eat World, *The Middle* | 2001 | Emo goes mainstream. |
| My Chemical Romance, *Helena* | 2004 | Half-time sections against fast ones. |
| Paramore, *Misery Business* | 2007 | Palm-muted riffing under a strong vocal. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Machine Gun Kelly, *bloody valentine* | 2020 | The pop-punk revival. |
| Olivia Rodrigo, *good 4 u* | 2021 | Pop-punk verse-to-chorus lift on a number one record. |

#### Sources

- Andy Greenwald, *Nothing Feels Good: Punk Rock, Teenagers, and Emo* (St. Martin's, 2003).
- Chris Payne, *Where Are Your Boys Tonight? The Oral History of Emo's Mainstream Explosion* (Dey St., 2023).

### Acoustic strum {#strum}

*A steel-string guitar over a light backbeat*

[Open the Acoustic strum style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=strum){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The singer-songwriter's band: a steel-string acoustic guitar strumming a syncopated pattern (down, down-up,
up-down-up), a bass and kick together on 1, the and of 2, and 3, and a light backbeat.

#### A little history

The steel-string guitar became a popular accompanying instrument through country and blues players in the
1920s-30s and the folk revival of the 1950s-60s (Woody Guthrie, then Bob Dylan, Joan Baez). From the
late 1960s singer-songwriters (James Taylor, Joni Mitchell, Cat Stevens) put a band around the strummed
guitar. The 1990s Britpop and "unplugged" years (Oasis's *Wonderwall*) and the 2000s-2010s folk-pop of
Jason Mraz, Mumford & Sons and Ed Sheeran kept it among the most common sounds in pop.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Dotted (1, and of 2, 3)*, with the kick. **Comping:** a campfire strum. **Drums:** light.

#### Listening

|---|---|---|

| Tom Petty, *Free Fallin'* | 1989 | Twelve-string strum, the band joining bit by bit. |
| Oasis, *Wonderwall* | 1995 | The syncopated strum everyone learned. |
| Jason Mraz, *I'm Yours* | 2008 | A reggae-tinged strum. |
| Ed Sheeran, *Thinking Out Loud* | 2014 | Acoustic guitar at the centre of a pop record. |

### Piano ballad {#pop}

*Left-hand octaves, a broken right hand, half-time drums*

[Open the Piano ballad style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=pop){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The slow pop or rock song led from the piano: octaves in the left hand, the chord broken or rocked in
the right (often in first inversion, so the top moves smoothly), and a band that comes in half-time, with
the backbeat on beat 3.

#### A little history

The piano was the home instrument of popular song long before rock: Tin Pan Alley sold sheet music for
it. In the 1970s singer-songwriters at the piano (Carole King's *Tapestry*, 1971; Elton John; Billy Joel)
made the piano ballad a staple of rock. The 1980s power ballad put it under big drums, and from the 2000s
Coldplay, Alicia Keys and Adele (*Someone Like You*, 2011, over nothing but broken piano chords) kept it
at the top of the charts.

#### The band's version

- **Comping:** three right-hand patterns (rocking, half-broken, syncopated) in four-bar spans.
- **Bass and drums:** half time; a quiet kick and a cross-stick on 3. The hi-hat sits low.

#### Listening

|---|---|---|
| Elton John, *Your Song* | 1970 | Broken chords under the voice, the band joining softly. |
| Carole King, *So Far Away* | 1971 | A singer-songwriter's left hand and right hand. |
| Billy Joel, *She's Always a Woman* | 1977 | Rocking right-hand patterns. |
| Coldplay, *The Scientist* | 2002 | Piano figure first, half-time band later. |
| Adele, *Someone Like You* | 2011 | Broken chords and nothing else. |

##### More recent

| Olivia Rodrigo, *drivers license* | 2021 | Piano verses, half-time band in the bridge. |

#### Sources

- Philip Furia, *The Poets of Tin Pan Alley* (Oxford, 1990), on the piano and popular song.
- Carole King, *A Natural Woman: A Memoir* (Grand Central, 2012), on writing and playing *Tapestry*.

### Dance pop {#dance}

*Four on the floor, open hi-hat off-beats, octave bass*

[Open the Dance pop style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=dance){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The disco beat and its descendants: a kick drum on every beat (*four on the floor*), the open hi-hat on
every off-beat, a bass jumping between the root and its octave, and chords on a 3+3+2.

#### A little history

Disco grew out of New York and Philadelphia clubs in the early 1970s. Earl Young, the drummer of
Philadelphia International's house band MFSB, is often credited with the steady kick and open hi-hat
(*The Love I Lost*, Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, 1973). The octave bass became disco's other mark
(Chic's Bernard Edwards). Giorgio Moroder and Donna Summer's *I Feel Love* (1977) put the beat on
synthesizers and pointed toward house and techno (Chicago and Detroit, mid-1980s). Since then the
four-on-the-floor beat has stayed at the centre of dance pop: Madonna, Kylie Minogue, Daft Punk, Dua Lipa.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Octaves*. **Comping:** a 3+3+2, on the electric piano. **Drums:** four on the floor.

#### Listening

|---|---|---|
| Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, *The Love I Lost* | 1973 | Earl Young's kick and hi-hat. |
| Donna Summer, *I Feel Love* | 1977 | The beat on a sequencer. |
| Bee Gees, *Stayin' Alive* | 1977 | Disco at its most famous. |
| Chic, *Le Freak* | 1978 | Nile Rodgers' guitar, Bernard Edwards' bass. |
| Dua Lipa, *Don't Start Now* | 2019 | The octave bass, forty years on. |

##### More recent

|---|---|---|

| Doja Cat, *Say So* | 2019 | Disco revival: four on the floor, octave-style bass. |

#### Sources

- Alice Echols, *Hot Stuff: Disco and the Remaking of American Culture* (Norton, 2010).
- Tim Lawrence, *Love Saves the Day: A History of American Dance Music Culture, 1970-1979* (Duke, 2003).

### Motown / soul {#motown}

*Snare on every beat, tambourine on 2 and 4*

[Open the Motown / soul style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=motown){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The 1960s Detroit sound of Motown Records: a snare (often with a tambourine) hitting every beat, a busy
electric bass, guitars chopping chords, and a song built for radio and dancing.

#### A little history

Berry Gordy started Motown in Detroit in 1959. Its records were cut by a house band later known as the
**Funk Brothers**: drummer Benny Benjamin, bassist James Jamerson, pianist Earl Van Dyke, and others,
playing in Studio A ("the Snakepit"). The songwriting team Holland-Dozier-Holland wrote the mid-'60s run of
hits for the Supremes and the Four Tops, many on a stomping four-beat snare. Jamerson's bass lines,
played with one finger on a Fender Precision, moved far more than any pattern can show.
The band played uncredited until the film *Standing in the Shadows of Motown* (2002).

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Motown: root, fifth, octave*, a stand-in for Jamerson's lines.
- **Comping:** the two-bar rhythm of *You Can't Hurry Love*. **Drums:** snare on every beat.

#### Listening

| The Supremes, *Where Did Our Love Go* | 1964 | The stomp on every beat. |
| Four Tops, *I Can't Help Myself (Sugar Pie Honey Bunch)* | 1965 | Holland-Dozier-Holland at full speed. |
| The Supremes, *You Can't Hurry Love* | 1966 | The rhythm the band's comping copies. |
| Marvin Gaye & Tammi Terrell, *Ain't No Mountain High Enough* | 1967 | Jamerson's bass. |
| Martha and the Vandellas, *Heat Wave* | 1963 | Tambourine and snare driving every beat. |

| Duffy, *Mercy* | 2008 | A 60s soul beat on a 2000s hit. |

#### Sources

  (Hal Leonard, 1989).

### 12/8 doo-wop {#doowop}

*Triplet piano chords over a slow backbeat*

[Open the 12/8 doo-wop style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=doowop){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The slow 1950s ballad: piano chords repeated in triplets, three to every beat, over a slow backbeat,
usually on the *I-vi-IV-V* chords, behind a lead singer and vocal group.

#### A little history

**Doo-wop** came from African American vocal groups on street corners in New York, Philadelphia,
Baltimore and Chicago in the late 1940s and '50s, following the Ink Spots and the Mills Brothers. The
backing singers sang nonsense syllables (*doo-wop, sh-boom*) in place of instruments. On record, small
bands added a pianist hammering triplets, an idea from New Orleans rhythm and blues (Fats Domino) and
the slow blues. The same 12/8 feel carries soul ballads into the 1960s, from Etta James's *At Last* onward.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *12/8 ballad*. **Comping:** triplets. **Drums:** slow 12/8 backbeat.
- On a 4/4 chart the band plays the triplets over each beat.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Fats Domino, *Blueberry Hill* | 1956 | New Orleans triplet piano. |
| The Penguins, *Earth Angel* | 1954 | I-vi-IV-V and doo-wop backing voices. |
| The Platters, *Only You (And You Alone)* | 1955 | Triplets on the piano from the first bar. |
| The Five Satins, *In the Still of the Nite* | 1956 | *Shoo-doop shoobee-doo* backing. |
| Etta James, *At Last* | 1960 | The 12/8 ballad with strings. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Ed Sheeran, *Perfect* | 2017 | A slow 12/8: hear three pulses in every beat. |

#### Sources

- Stuart L. Goosman, *Group Harmony: The Black Urban Roots of Rhythm and Blues* (Penn, 2005).
- Anthony J. Gribin and Matthew M. Schiff, *The Complete Book of Doo-Wop* (Krause, 2000).

### Country train beat {#train}

*Boom-chicka strum and the snare on every eighth*

[Open the Country train beat style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=train){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The country rhythm that sounds like a steam train: a snare (often with brushes) on every eighth note,
accented on 2 and 4, a bass on root and fifth, and a *boom-chicka* guitar.

#### A little history

The sound is most associated with Johnny Cash's Tennessee Two at Sun Records in Memphis: Luther Perkins'
muted *boom-chicka* electric guitar and Marshall Grant's slapped bass on *Folsom Prison Blues* (1955) and
*I Walk the Line* (1956). Drummer W. S. Holland joined in 1960 and the train beat became a drum pattern.
Train songs had been part of country and blues since the 1920s (Jimmie Rodgers), and the beat has stayed
in rockabilly, bluegrass-flavoured country and country rock.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Root and fifth*. **Comping:** a boom-chicka strum. **Drums:** train beat.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Johnny Cash, *Folsom Prison Blues* | 1955 | Luther Perkins' boom-chicka; no drummer. |
| Johnny Cash, *I Walk the Line* | 1956 | The same band, the train feel without drums. |
| Johnny Cash, *Orange Blossom Special* | 1965 | A train song with the full band. |
| Merle Haggard, *Mama Tried* | 1968 | Bakersfield country on the beat. |
| Marty Stuart, *Hillbilly Rock* | 1989 | A later country rock version. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Dwight Yoakam, *Guitars, Cadillacs* | 1986 | Bakersfield country revival; the beat behind a twangy guitar. |

#### Sources

- Michael Streissguth, *Johnny Cash: The Biography* (Da Capo, 2006).
- Bill C. Malone, *Country Music, U.S.A.* (Texas, 3rd ed. 2010).

### Boom-chick {#folk}

*Bass on 1 and 3, chords on 2 and 4; oom-pah-pah in 3/4*

[Open the Boom-chick style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=folk){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The oldest accompaniment in popular music: a bass note on the strong beats and a chord on the weak ones.
In 2/4 or 4/4 it is *boom-chick*; in 3/4 it is *oom-pah-pah*.

#### A little history

Brass bands and dance orchestras of the 1800s split the beat between the tuba (or bass) and the horns or
second violins: marches, polkas and waltzes all run on it, and so does the stride and ragtime piano left
hand (bass note, chord, bass note, chord). Guitarists in American old-time and country music used the same
idea, a thumbed bass on the beat and a strum after it: Maybelle Carter's guitar with the Carter Family
from 1927, and later the folk revival. Sing-along songs from campfire to music hall still use it.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Root and fifth*. **Comping:** *oompah*. **Drums:** boom-chick.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Scott Joplin, *Maple Leaf Rag* (many recordings) | 1899 | The boom-chick in a ragtime left hand. |
| The Carter Family, *Can the Circle Be Unbroken* | 1935 | Maybelle Carter's bass and strum. |
| Woody Guthrie, *This Land Is Your Land* | 1944 rec. | Folk guitar boom-chick. |
| Hank Williams, *Jambalaya (On the Bayou)* | 1952 | Country two-beat. |
| Frankie Yankovic, *Blue Skirt Waltz* | 1949 | Oom-pah-pah with accordion. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Old Crow Medicine Show, *Wagon Wheel* | 2004 | Boom-chick under a sing-along. |
| Mumford & Sons, *Little Lion Man* | 2009 | Banjo and kick drum on the boom-chick. |
| The Lumineers, *Ho Hey* | 2012 | Kick on the beat, guitar and claps after it. |

#### Sources

- Bill C. Malone, *Country Music, U.S.A.* (Texas, 3rd ed. 2010).
- [Wikipedia, *Can the Circle Be Unbroken*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can_the_Circle_Be_Unbroken_(By_and_By)): recorded 6 May 1935.
- Edward A. Berlin, *Ragtime: A Musical and Cultural History* (California, 1980).

### Freylekhs / polka {#freylekhs}

*Bass on every beat, the whole chord on every off-beat*

[Open the Freylekhs / polka style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=freylekhs){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

The fast 2/4 of Eastern European dance music: the bass on every beat, alternating root and fifth, and the
full chord on every off-beat (*oom-pa oom-pa*). A **freylekhs** ("joyful") is the most common klezmer
dance tune; the **polka** is its Central European cousin.

#### A little history

The **polka** started in Bohemia in the 1830s and was danced across Europe and America within a decade. Its
bands (brass, then accordion) gave it the bass-and-off-beat accompaniment. **Klezmer** is the instrumental
music of Ashkenazi Jewish weddings in Eastern Europe. Immigrant clarinettists Naftule Brandwein and Dave
Tarras recorded it in New York in the 1920s, with bands that played the same driving off-beats on piano,
brass and drums. It faded after the war and came back in the 1970s revival (the Klezmorim, Andy Statman,
Kapelye, later the Klezmatics). Songs like *Hava Nagila* and Hanukkah songs are still played this way.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Root and fifth on every beat*, with a run up into the next bar now and then.
- **Comping:** chords on the off-beats. In half-time bars the piano switches to ballad patterns.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Naftule Brandwein, *Der Heyser Bulgar* | 1923 | Clarinet over off-beat backing. |
| Dave Tarras, *Dave Tarras' Freylekhs* (many dance sides) | 1920s-50s | New York klezmer dance band. |
| Frankie Yankovic, *Just Because* | 1947 | American polka. |
| The Klezmatics, *Rhythm + Jews* | 1991 | Revival klezmer. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Gogol Bordello, *Start Wearing Purple* | 2005 | Eastern European off-beats as punk. |
| "Weird Al" Yankovic, *Polka Face* (*Alpocalypse*) | 2011 | A polka medley of pop hits: bass on the beat, chords off it. |

#### Sources

- Henry Sapoznik, *Klezmer! Jewish Music from Old World to Our World* (Schirmer, 1999; 2nd ed. 2006).
- Walter Zev Feldman, *Klezmer: Music, History, and Memory* (Oxford, 2016).
- [DAHR, Naftule Brandwein](https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/names/111839): *Heiser bulgar*, Victor, 10 May 1923.
- Victor Greene, *A Passion for Polka* (California, 1992).

### John Prine Fingerpicking {#prine}

*Thumb on alternating bass strings, fingers pinching on 2 and 4*

[Open the John Prine Fingerpicking style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=prine){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

A steel-string guitar played with the thumb and fingers at once: the thumb alternates between two bass
strings on every beat while the fingers pluck the chord on the off-beats or pinch with the thumb. No drums,
an upright bass doubling the thumb.

#### A little history

Alternating-thumb picking runs back to Black guitarists in the South of the 1920s: Mississippi John Hurt
recorded for OKeh in 1928, and Elizabeth Cotten played *Freight Train* left-handed. In Kentucky, Arnold
Shultz, Ike Everly and Mose Rager handed it to **Merle Travis**, after whom "Travis picking" is named, and
Chet Atkins spread it through country guitar. The 1960s folk revival brought it to singer-songwriters.
**John Prine** (1946-2020), the Chicago postman whose first album (*John Prine*, 1971) contains *Paradise*,
*Hello in There* and *Angel from Montgomery*, played a plain thumb-and-fingers style under plain-spoken songs.

#### The band's version

- **Comping:** the *prine* and *travis* patterns. **Bass:** root and fifth with the thumb. **Drums:** none.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Mississippi John Hurt, *Candy Man Blues* | 1928 | Steady alternating thumb. |
| Merle Travis, *Cannonball Rag* | 1940s | Travis picking itself. |
| Elizabeth Cotten, *Freight Train* | late 1950s | The folk-revival classic. |
| John Prine, *Paradise* (*John Prine*) | 1971 | The style the band copies. |
| John Prine, *Angel from Montgomery* (*John Prine*) | 1971 | Thumb and fingers under a slow song. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Jason Isbell, *Elephant* | 2013 | A fingerpicked song from one of Prine's heirs. |
| Taylor Swift, *invisible string* (*folklore*) | 2020 | Thumb-and-fingers guitar under a pop song. |

#### Sources

- Eddie Huffman, *John Prine: In Spite of Himself* (Texas, 2015).
- Bobby Anderson, *That Muhlenberg Sound* (1993), on Shultz, Rager and Travis.

## Hymns and carols

### Waltz (in one) {#waltz}

*A quick 3/4 felt one to the bar*

[Open the Waltz (in one) style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=waltz){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

A fast 3/4 in which the listener feels one beat a bar, not three: the bass on 1, light chords on 2 and 3,
brushes, bars grouped in fours.

#### A little history

The waltz rose from Austrian and South German country dances in the late 1700s and took over the ballrooms
of Vienna in the early 1800s with Joseph Lanner and the Strauss family (Johann Strauss II's *The Blue
Danube*, 1867). Played fast, the pulse is one per bar, and phrases come in fours and eights. The waltz then
spread everywhere: music-hall and parlour songs, country waltzes (*Tennessee Waltz*), jazz waltzes, and
many carols and folk songs that are sung in a quick 3/4.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** root on 1 (root one bar, fifth the next). **Comping:** *waltz*. **Drums:** brushed waltz.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Johann Strauss II, *The Blue Danube* (any Vienna Philharmonic recording) | 1867 | The Viennese waltz, the second beat slightly early. |
| Bill Monroe, *Kentucky Waltz* | 1946 (not checked) | A country waltz. |
| Patti Page, *Tennessee Waltz* | 1950 | A pop hit in 3/4. |
| Bill Evans, *Waltz for Debby* | 1961 | Jazz waltz, for contrast. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Billy Joel, *Piano Man* | 1973 | A pop song in 3/4, the bass on 1. |
| Norah Jones, *Come Away With Me* | 2002 | A slower 3/4, for contrast with the waltz in one. |

#### Sources

- Eduard Reeser, *The History of the Waltz* (1949); Mosco Carner, *The Waltz* (1948).

### Hymn (four parts) {#hymn}

*Every chord held until the next, the bass doubling the root*

[Open the Hymn (four parts) style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=hymn){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Congregational hymn accompaniment: soprano, alto, tenor and bass moving together, one chord per melody
note or two, each held until the next, no drums. The organ is the obvious instrument.

#### A little history

Martin Luther's chorales (from the 1520s) gave Protestant congregations hymns to sing; J. S. Bach's
four-part harmonisations of them in his cantatas and passions (1720s-40s) became the model of how to
write harmony, and still are in theory classes. In England, Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley in the 1700s
wrote the texts; the collection *Hymns Ancient and Modern* (1861) and *The English Hymnal* (1906, music
edited by Ralph Vaughan Williams) set the four-part style of the Anglican hymnal. American hymnals, gospel
song and shape-note singing grew from the same roots.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Held roots*. **Comping:** *hymn*: three voices over the root. **Drums:** none.
- Choose Church organ as the instrument for the other obvious sound.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| J. S. Bach, *Wachet auf* chorale (Cantata 140, final movement) | 1731 | Four-part chorale. |
| Choir of King's College, Cambridge, *Once in Royal David's City* | any year | The hymn that opens their Christmas Eve service. |
| Vaughan Williams, *Down Ampney* (*Come Down, O Love Divine*) | 1906 | An English Hymnal tune. |
| Any congregational recording of *Old Hundredth* | 1551 tune | The oldest hymn tune still in common use. |

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Keith Getty & Stuart Townend, *In Christ Alone* | 2001 | A modern hymn, often sung in four parts. |
| Chris Tomlin, *Amazing Grace (My Chains Are Gone)* | 2006 | An old hymn tune with a band. |

#### Sources

- Erik Routley, *The Music of Christian Hymns* (GIA, 1981).
- J. R. Watson, *The English Hymn* (Oxford, 1997).

### Folk carol {#carol}

*Strummed guitar, bass on 1 and 3, very light time*

[Open the Folk carol style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=carol){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

#### What it is

Traditional carols played by a folk-rock band: a strummed steel-string guitar, upright bass on 1 and 3,
light brushes. Between the four-part [hymn](#hymn) and [acoustic strum](#strum).

#### A little history

Many English carols are older than the hymns sung beside them: dance songs and wassails collected by
Cecil Sharp and Ralph Vaughan Williams in the early 1900s and published in *The Oxford Book of Carols*
(1928). The British folk revival of the 1960s and the folk-rock bands that followed (Steeleye Span,
Fairport Convention) played them with guitars, fiddles and drums, and many carol albums since have done
the same.

#### The band's version

- **Bass:** *Roots on 1 and 3*. **Comping:** folk strum. **Drums:** brushes, very light.

#### Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| The Watersons, *Frost and Fire* | 1965 | Unaccompanied ritual songs and carols: the source material. |
| Steeleye Span, *Gaudete* | 1973 | A Latin carol in a folk-rock band's hands (sung unaccompanied). |
| Jethro Tull, *Ring Out, Solstice Bells* | 1976 | Folk rock for Christmas. |
| Sufjan Stevens, *Songs for Christmas* | 2006 | Traditional carols with banjo and guitar. |

Track details on this page have not been checked against discographies yet.

##### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Sufjan Stevens, *O Come O Come Emmanuel* (*Songs for Christmas*) | 2006 | A folk-band carol (album already listed above). |

#### Sources

- Rob Young, *Electric Eden: Unearthing Britain's Visionary Music* (Faber, 2010).
